summary: Believers as God’s children, a relational benefit distinct from justification; inheritance and intimacy
readingInstruction: Read Romans 8:14-17, Galatians 4:1-7, and 1 John 3:1-3. Today is a doctrinal pause on adoption. Notice who does the adopting, what the Spirit cries, and what the adopted child receives.
settingTheScene: Adoption was a familiar practice in the Roman world. A wealthy family without a suitable heir could adopt a son, who then gained the full rights of the family name and inheritance. Paul uses this to explain what God has done for believers. We were not born children of God in the full covenant sense; we were slaves, and God brought us into his family at great cost. John, the apostle of love, marvels at the same fact.
observation: “For all who are led by the Spirit of God are sons of God” (Romans 8:14).
“You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, by whom we cry, Abba! Father!” (Romans 8:15).
“And if children, then heirs, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ” (Romans 8:17).

“But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son, born of woman, born under the law, to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons” (Galatians 4:4-5).
“And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba! Father!” (Galatians 4:6).
“So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God” (Galatians 4:7).
“See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are” (1 John 3:1).
“Beloved, we are God’s children now” (1 John 3:2).
doctrinalFocus:
Adoption is the act of God by which he receives believers into his family as his sons and daughters, with all the rights and privileges that belong to children. It is one of the richest images of salvation. Justification answers the question, “How can I be declared right before the Judge?” Adoption answers the question, “How can I be welcomed by the Father?” The two go together. Justification gives us a legal standing; adoption gives us a family and a Father.

Notice the Trinity at work. The Father sends the Son “in the fullness of time” to redeem those under the law. The Son becomes man, born of woman, born under the law, so that he can redeem. The Spirit is sent into our hearts, and he teaches us to cry “Abba! Father!” The word Abba is the Aramaic word of a child to his father, an intimate word that Jesus himself used in Gethsemane (Mark 14:36). Through Christ we share his relationship with the Father.

Adoption has present and future dimensions. Now we are God’s children, and we have the Spirit, access to the Father, his discipline, his care, and his promises. But Paul also says we “wait eagerly for adoption as sons, the redemption of our bodies” (Romans 8:23). Our full inheritance, the resurrection and the new creation, is still to come. John says, “What we will be has not yet appeared; but we know that when he appears we will be like him.”

Adoption is the answer to many fears. The fear of rejection: God has chosen you. The fear of earning: a child does not earn his place. The fear of being alone: the Father is near. And the fear of failing: a child may fail, but remains a child. It also shapes our life together: if we have one Father, we are brothers and sisters. Christians who struggle with the idea of God as Father, because of a human father who failed them, can find that God is the Father they always needed.
interpretation:
Galatians 4 begins with an illustration. An heir, as long as he is a child, is no different from a slave, though he is the owner of everything. He is under guardians until the date set by his father. So we, when we were children, were enslaved to the elementary principles of the world. “But when the fullness of time had come, God sent forth his Son.” The timing was God’s. He sent his Son “born of woman, born under the law.” The Son took on humanity and submitted to the law. The purpose: “to redeem those who were under the law, so that we might receive adoption as sons.”

Then the Spirit: “And because you are sons, God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, Abba! Father!” The Spirit is the Spirit of the Son; when he lives in us, he leads us to pray as the Son prays. Prayer is the family voice. “So you are no longer a slave, but a son, and if a son, then an heir through God.”

Romans 8 gives the same truth in the setting of suffering. The Spirit does not make us slaves again to fall back into fear, but sons. “The Spirit himself bears witness with our spirit that we are children of God, and if children, then heirs, heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ, provided we suffer with him in order that we may also be glorified with him.” We share his sufferings now and his glory later.

1 John 3:1 sounds like a gasp of wonder: “See what kind of love the Father has given to us, that we should be called children of God; and so we are.” The love is not just a feeling; it is something given, an action. And the “so we are” is a guarantee. The world does not recognize us, because it did not know him. But the hope is certain: when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is. And “everyone who thus hopes in him purifies himself as he is pure.” The hope of the family inheritance motivates holy living.
connection: Mark 14:36 records Jesus praying “Abba, Father.” Matthew 6:9 begins the Lord’s Prayer with “Our Father.” John 1:12-13 says to all who believed he gave the right to become children of God. Ephesians 1:5 speaks of predestination to adoption. Hebrews 12:5-11 speaks of the Father’s discipline. Romans 8:23 and 9:4 speak of adoption. 2 Corinthians 6:18 quotes the promise “I will be a father to you.” Luke 15:11-32 shows the Father’s welcome. Revelation 21:7 says the one who conquers will have this heritage.
application:
Pray “Abba, Father” today and let yourself feel what it means.

If you struggle with the word “Father,” tell God honestly. Ask him to show you what a true Father is.

Treat a fellow believer today as a brother or sister, not an acquaintance.
prayerPrompts: Thank God for sending his Son to redeem you so that you could be adopted.
Pray, “Abba, Father,” and tell him what it means.
Thank him that you are an heir.
